\title[Improving Evidence Retrieval for Scientific Claim Verification]{Improving Evidence Retrieval for Scientific Claim Verification: In-Domain Fine-Tuning with Analytically Weighted Rank Fusion}
\author[1]{\fnm{Pooja} \sur{Gupta}}\email{pooja.gupta@jaipur.manipal.edu}
\author[1]{\fnm{Vivansh} \sur{Garg}}\email{vivanshgarg05@gmail.com}
\affil[1]{\orgdiv{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (Data Science)}, \orgname{Manipal University Jaipur}, \orgaddress{\city{Jaipur}, \state{Rajasthan}, \country{India}}}

\abstract{Literature assistants such as SciSpace and Consensus answer scientific questions with citations, but each answer depends on one step they do not expose: which is finding the right evidence. This paper takes only that step and improves it. A small sentence encoder is fine-tuned on scientific claims and is fused with keyword search (BM25) at a weight chosen on held-out claims, and the cross-encoder reranker of the standard hybrid pipeline is also removed. We prove, that below a BM25 weight of $61/160 \approx 0.38$, reciprocal rank fusion can only re-order the dense retriever's candidates, this also explains why the chosen weight works. On SciFact (300 test claims with known evidence) the improved retrieval reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.759 against 0.715 for the standard pipeline ($p = 0.003$), which is at about a third of the time per claim. On a second dataset, NFCorpus, it is statistically level with the reranked pipeline (0.350 against 0.358, $p = 0.35$) at a sixth of the time, while fine-tuning helps less on its lay queries. A failure analysis performed shows that 42\% of the hardest misses are evidence the benchmark marks but that does not state the claim, and that the improvement repairs 22 of the 40 hardest failures.}

\keywords{evidence retrieval, scientific claim verification, hybrid retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, dense retrieval, fine-tuning, cross-encoder reranking}

\section*{Declarations}

\paragraph{Ethical approval} Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants,
human data, or animal experiments; it uses only publicly available benchmark datasets of
published scientific abstracts and queries.

\paragraph{Consent to participate} Not applicable. This study did not involve human
participants.

\paragraph{Consent to publish} Not applicable. This study does not contain any individual
person's data in any form.

\paragraph{Competing interests} The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

\paragraph{Data availability} The datasets analysed during the current study are publicly
available: SciFact \parencite{wadden2020scifact} and NFCorpus \parencite{boteva2016nfcorpus},
both obtained through the BEIR benchmark \parencite{thakur2021beir}. The code, configuration
files and result files generated during the study are available from the authors on
reasonable request.

\paragraph{Author contributions} Vivansh Garg implemented the system, carried out the
experiments and the analysis, and wrote the manuscript. Pooja Gupta supervised the work and
reviewed the manuscript. Both authors read and approved the final manuscript.

\paragraph{Funding} No funding was received for this study.

\paragraph{Use of generative AI} Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to assist with
code development, running the experiments and drafting the manuscript. The authors take full
